10.text: and at Indian Point, they are in the immediate vicinity of the present habitations,

11.text: and the villagers still remember to what families most of the ruins belong.

12.text: As before mentioned, they claim that these houses went out of use three

13.text: generations ago. At the time of Hooper’s visit in 1848, houses of the modern

14.text: type were already in use, and he mentions having seen half-ruined underground

15.text: houses which were in no better condition when I found them, fifty-two years

16.text: later. The waˊlkar of the Maritime Chukchee and Asiatic Eskimo had a
16.note: mz keyed the stress mark as '/'; raster shows U+02CA per §2.1/§4 default.

17.text: frame made of jaw-bones. Heavy pieces were set in the ground in an upright

18.text: position at intervals all around the house, and were held in place by earth

19.text: and stones. Sometimes there were about sixteen of these supports, so that

20.text: they formed a regular fence. Large pieces of jaw-bone or of whale’s ribs

21.text: were superposed as rafters, and smaller pieces were inserted to make the

22.text: structure more compact. The floor, or at least the middle part of it, was

23.text: paved with flat pieces of bone. Then the whole structure was covered with

24.text: sod, and a thick layer of loose earth was strewn around the bottom. Often

25.text: the waˊlkar was started with a circular excavation, and, after being well covered
25.note: mz keyed the stress mark as '/'; raster shows U+02CA per §2.1/§4 default.

26.text: with earth, appeared to be a half-underground house, with only the roof pro-

27.text: truding above the surface. Even the “jaw-bone houses” built above ground,

28.text: in the course of a long period of time, assumed the shape of small hillocks,

34.text: in the hardened earth supports its walls (Fig. 100). Most of the uprights

35.text: which support the side-walls are formed of two parts, the upper being thinner

36.text: than that below. The upper parts are not fastened to those below, but are

37.text: firmly implanted on their top. The pressure of the rafters, and the weight

38.text: of the soil which covers the structure, help to hold them in place. The

39.text: roof is formed of several curved beams, which rest on other uprights,

40.text: short and stout, leaned against the front and the rear wall (Plate XVIII,

41.text: Figs. 2, 3). Like the underground house of other tribes, it has two entrances.

42.text: One is through a long underground passage, and could be used only in
